1. Scan: position and probe
Position
Supine, head turned away, arm by the side. Donut under the head to create space for the needle.
Probe
High-frequency linear probe, transverse (axial) across the neck at the level of C6.
Landmark
Interscalene groove at the level of C6 (cricoid cartilage). Probe transverse to the neck: identify the common carotid artery, then scan laterally.
Screen orientation
Left of screen = Ant / Med; right = Post / Lat.
Field shown
52 mm wide, 32 mm deep (to scale).
Pearls
If the anatomy at C6 is ambiguous, use the "traceback" technique: find the plexus in the supraclavicular fossa and slide cephalad until the cluster separates into roots between the scalenes.
Use colour Doppler for the vertebral artery and other neck vessels; the neck is vascular.
Beware other branches in the needle path: dorsal scapular and long thoracic nerves in the middle scalene.
Level check: C6 has the prominent anterior (Chassaignac) tubercle; C7 has a deficient anterior tubercle because the vertebral artery enters the transverse foramen at C6.
Superior trunk block: start interscalene and scan caudally until C5 and C6 join; the trunk is often superficial to the anterior scalene. Good for shoulder surgery with a lower risk of phrenic palsy.
Aim the needle between the roots, never straight at one. If the tip touches a root, injection pressure rises: withdraw slightly before injecting.
C6 (and C7) often look split into two circles. Do not inject between the two halves of one root, which risks an intraneural injection: inject between C5 and C6, superficial to C5 or deep to C6.
Variant: the C5 root can run through the anterior scalene for part of its course. Follow it distally until it enters the interscalene groove.
After the first 5–7 ml, keep the needle still and slide the probe down to the supraclavicular fossa: local anaesthetic around the trunks there confirms you injected in the right compartment.
Patient set-up: head up slightly (less prominent neck veins), and ask the patient to reach towards the knee on the same side to drop the shoulder and give more room.
Never perform bilateral interscalene blocks (risk of bilateral phrenic palsy).
If phrenic palsy matters, options are a lower volume (about 5 ml, at some cost to duration and success), a lower injection around C7, a superior trunk block, combined suprascapular and axillary nerve blocks, or a supraclavicular block. Check the diaphragm with ultrasound (M-mode, curvilinear probe under the costal margin) if in doubt.

Expected side effect: Phrenic nerve block.

INDICATIONS

Upper arm and shoulder surgery, e.g. shoulder arthroscopy, total shoulder arthroplasty, proximal humerus fractures.

COMPLICATIONS
Phrenic nerve block causing hemidiaphragmatic paresis (caution / contraindication in significant respiratory disease)
Horner’s syndrome (cervical sympathetic chain)
Recurrent laryngeal nerve block (hoarseness)
Epidural spread or total spinal anaesthesia
Pneumothorax
Vertebral artery puncture or intravascular injection: seizures / local anaesthetic systemic toxicity
Bezold–Jarisch reflex (bradycardia and hypotension) in the sitting / beach-chair position
Rarely, phrenic nerve palsy persists after the block wears off (thought to be inflammation or entrapment rather than needle trauma)

Check the diaphragm with ultrasound (M-mode, curvilinear probe under the costal margin) if in doubt.
EXAM QUESTIONS
Q1 Perform the block and name the structures. You are asked to scan medially: what do you see?

Common carotid artery and internal jugular vein medial to the scalenes; anterior and middle scalene with the C5/C6 "traffic light" between them; sternocleidomastoid superficially.

Q2 After an interscalene block the patient becomes dyspnoeic. Differentials?

Phrenic nerve palsy (most common); pneumothorax; high spinal / epidural spread with respiratory muscle weakness; recurrent laryngeal nerve block (can feel like dyspnoea); anaphylaxis.

Q3 The patient becomes hypotensive just before knife-to-skin for shoulder surgery. Differentials?

Bezold–Jarisch reflex in the beach-chair position (bradycardia and hypotension); high spinal / epidural spread; intravascular injection / LAST; anaphylaxis.

Q4 Which part of the plexus does an interscalene block target, and what is typically spared?

The roots (mainly C5–C6, often C7). C8–T1 is commonly spared, so the ulnar territory is missed.

Position
Supine, head turned away, arm by the side. Donut under the head to create space for the needle.
Probe
High-frequency linear probe, transverse (axial) across the neck at the level of C6.
Landmark
Interscalene groove at the level of C6 (cricoid cartilage). Probe transverse to the neck: identify the common carotid artery, then scan laterally.

Pearls
If the anatomy at C6 is ambiguous, use the "traceback" technique: find the plexus in the supraclavicular fossa and slide cephalad until the cluster separates into roots between the scalenes.
Use colour Doppler for the vertebral artery and other neck vessels; the neck is vascular.
Beware other branches in the needle path: dorsal scapular and long thoracic nerves in the middle scalene.
Level check: C6 has the prominent anterior (Chassaignac) tubercle; C7 has a deficient anterior tubercle because the vertebral artery enters the transverse foramen at C6.
Superior trunk block: start interscalene and scan caudally until C5 and C6 join; the trunk is often superficial to the anterior scalene. Good for shoulder surgery with a lower risk of phrenic palsy.
Aim the needle between the roots, never straight at one. If the tip touches a root, injection pressure rises: withdraw slightly before injecting.
C6 (and C7) often look split into two circles. Do not inject between the two halves of one root, which risks an intraneural injection: inject between C5 and C6, superficial to C5 or deep to C6.
Variant: the C5 root can run through the anterior scalene for part of its course. Follow it distally until it enters the interscalene groove.
After the first 5–7 ml, keep the needle still and slide the probe down to the supraclavicular fossa: local anaesthetic around the trunks there confirms you injected in the right compartment.
Patient set-up: head up slightly (less prominent neck veins), and ask the patient to reach towards the knee on the same side to drop the shoulder and give more room.
Never perform bilateral interscalene blocks (risk of bilateral phrenic palsy).
If phrenic palsy matters, options are a lower volume (about 5 ml, at some cost to duration and success), a lower injection around C7, a superior trunk block, combined suprascapular and axillary nerve blocks, or a supraclavicular block. Check the diaphragm with ultrasound (M-mode, curvilinear probe under the costal margin) if in doubt.

Supplement with…
Shoulder surgery: not suitable (suprascapular nerve spared).
Tourniquet or upper medial arm: add intercostobrachial infiltration.
Spread not reaching the medial cord: reposition, as for the coracoid infraclavicular block.
